  "text": "The station clock had stopped at eleven minutes past four, which meant Edith caught her train on time twice a day.

“Someone ought to mend it,” she told the man sweeping the platform.

“Someone's been informed,” he said.

“Are you someone?”

“Only when there's sweeping.”

His name was Alan. He had worked at the station for thirty years and carried spare gloves in case the weather changed its mind.

The following Thursday, Edith brought a small clock in a biscuit tin.

“For the waiting room,” she said.

Alan examined it. The face was decorated with roses.

“Does it keep good time?”

“It kept my sister punctual. No easy task.”

They put it on the windowsill beside a leaflet advertising a bus service that no longer existed.

The ticking filled the room pleasantly.

“Needs a biscuit,” Alan said.

“What does?”

“The tin. Looks disappointed.”

Edith returned the next week with shortbread.

By November, passengers had begun checking the little clock instead of the large one. Someone left a paperback beside it. Someone else added a cushion to the bench.

Then an engineer arrived and repaired the station clock.

Alan found Edith in the waiting room, wrapping her clock in a scarf.

“You could leave it,” he said.

“They'll disagree eventually.”

“We're used to that. We have two timetables.”

She unwrapped it and set it back among the crumbs.

Outside, the train pulled in.

“That's yours,” Alan said.

“I know.”

But she took a moment to wind the clock before she went."
